stories.title: Whatcha lookin’ at? Social anxiety heightens brain sensitivity to others’ gaze
stories.summary: A University of Michigan study found young adults with higher social anxiety showed stronger brain responses to mismatched social cues, specifically when a word describing thoughts or feelings didn't align with a gaze. This neural sensitivity (N400 response) did not improve their explicit judgments of gaze meaning, suggesting potential for increased rumination rather than better social insight.
stories.finding: A University of Michigan study found young adults with higher social anxiety showed stronger brain responses to mismatched social cues, specifically when a word describing thoughts or feelings didn't align with a gaze. This neural sensitivity (N400 response) did not improve their explicit judgments of gaze meaning, suggesting potential for increased rumination rather than better social insight.
stories.significance: This finding suggests that social anxiety may involve heightened neural sensitivity to social cues, offering a new perspective on social anxiety beyond just distress. This sensitivity could potentially be beneficial in certain social contexts, but also contribute to excessive worry.
stories.caveat: While individuals with higher social anxiety showed greater neural sensitivity, this did not translate to improved accuracy or speed in their explicit judgments about the meaning of a gaze. The study also did not establish whether this sensitivity helps people navigate real-world social situations.
stories.localConnection: University of Michigan research in Ann Arbor.

editorial.reason: New research from a local university (U-M) on a common psychological condition, offering a novel perspective on brain responses in social anxiety.

stories.title: They get knocked down—but they get up again
stories.summary: University of Michigan researchers found that low doses of the herbicide dicamba can cause oxalis weeds to produce more flowers, a phenomenon known as hormesis. While this did not consistently lead to increased seed production or genetic changes in the weed population, it altered pollinator visitation patterns and flower size.
stories.finding: University of Michigan researchers found that low doses of the herbicide dicamba can cause oxalis weeds to produce more flowers, a phenomenon known as hormesis. While this did not consistently lead to increased seed production or genetic changes in the weed population, it altered pollinator visitation patterns and flower size.
stories.significance: This finding suggests that the inadvertent drift of herbicides at low concentrations might be making weeds more robust, rather than eliminating them, potentially impacting agricultural practices and lawn care.
stories.caveat: The study found no evidence that the increased flower production trait was heritable or would evolve in the oxalis population, and the increased flower production did not consistently translate to increased seed production in the second year of the experiment. Additionally, plants with more flowers due to dicamba exposure had lower pollinator visitation rates.
stories.localConnection: University of Michigan research in Ann Arbor.

stories.title: Mollusk microbiome? It’s all in the family
stories.summary: University of Michigan researchers found that mollusk microbiome composition is primarily determined by species rather than environment, based on a review of 85 studies. This suggests that genetic lineage, or "family tree," is more influential than habitat in shaping these microbial communities, which aid digestion and protection.
stories.finding: University of Michigan researchers found that mollusk microbiome composition is primarily determined by species rather than environment, based on a review of 85 studies. This suggests that genetic lineage, or "family tree," is more influential than habitat in shaping these microbial communities, which aid digestion and protection.
stories.significance: Understanding the factors that shape mollusk microbiomes is crucial for predicting how these populations will respond to environmental changes, such as pollution or rising temperatures. This knowledge can help in preventing mollusk die-offs, which are important for ecosystem health.
stories.caveat: The study highlights a significant gap in research, noting that most studies focus on edible mollusk species and are concentrated in specific geographic regions. This human-centered research limits the understanding of the vast diversity of mollusk microbiomes and their responses to environmental changes.
stories.localConnection: University of Michigan research in Ann Arbor.

inputFacts.title: Mollusk microbiome? It’s all in the family
inputFacts.summary: The composition of a mollusk's microbiome is primarily determined by its species (family tree) rather than its living environment. This means that mollusks of the same species will have more similar microbiomes, even if they live in different locations, than mollusks of different species living in the same environment.
inputFacts.finding: The composition of a mollusk's microbiome is primarily determined by its species (family tree) rather than its living environment. This means that mollusks of the same species will have more similar microbiomes, even if they live in different locations, than mollusks of different species living in the same environment.

editorial.reason: Substantive new finding in biology from a local university, relevant to understanding ecosystem health.
editorial.groundingReason: University of Michigan researchers conducted a review of 85 studies to determine that mollusk microbiome composition is primarily determined by species rather than environment, a new finding in the field.

inputFacts.summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope has observed that brown dwarfs possess chemically rich atmospheres containing water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methane, similar to giant planets in our solar system.

inputFacts.summary: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, with NASA's support, is planned to launch in October 2026 to characterize and determine the origin of Mars' moons Phobos and Deimos and return a sample of Phobos to Earth.

inputFacts.title: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
inputFacts.summary: NASA satellites have observed the unfolding of a historic El Niño event in 2026, characterized by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in the equatorial Pacific, rising sea surface heights, and changes in ocean color due to decreased phytoplankton abundance.

inputFacts.title: Many older adults make Medicare decisions quickly, most don’t change plans
inputFacts.summary: A University of Michigan survey found that 60% of older adults spend less than an hour choosing their Medicare coverage during Open Enrollment, with 27% not reviewing options at all, and 80% retaining their previous year's coverage.

inputFacts.title: NSF lays the foundation for the next generation of technologies and support for American talent
inputFacts.summary: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) is launching several new programs and initiatives, including an Office of Metascience, two Grand Research Challenge (GRC) prize competitions (Quantum+X GRC and Synthetic Multicellularity Grand Challenge), the NSF X-Labs Consortium, and a funding opportunity for Super Intelligence-Native Instruments (SINI) within the NSF Programmable Cloud Laboratories Network (NSF PCLNet). Additionally, NSF is investing in the National Math Stars and NextGen Workforce programs.

inputFacts.title: NSF–UKRI metascience statement
